articleTitle: A new engineering profession is emerging: decision coach
abstract: More than half of the decisions faced by corporate executives deal with expansion or investment in new and existing products, services, or geographies. These decisions are complicated technically and organizationally. As a result, the decisions tend to be made by teams from multiple functions: research, engineering, marketing, sales, manufacturing, public relations, and legal. Strategic decision making has become a team sport. Teams need coaches to help pick the right processes; apply the right tools; facilitate learning; and manage projects. This article is about an emerging profession: decision coach. The article explains why most decision coaches will probably begin their coaching careers as decision engineers.

articleTitle: Technology: The forgotten science
abstract: The purpose of this article is to promote the more effective use of technology, not only at the level of technological detail, but also at the level of corporate guidance and national policy. Only a small minority of technology professionals and engineers are mindful today of the true origins of the technology concept. Technology was originally conceived as a body of knowledge organized into a scientific discipline that described purposeful action in industry. Technology management and policy are of the most challenging tasks facing specialists and engineers. This article suggests a new key for grasping technology. New, because the key that defined the science in the first place has been irretrievably lost. The situation is reminiscent of the story of the tower of Babel. According to this narrative a group of builders came together to construct a tower that would reach to the sky. They wished to interact with the master of the universe. The master feared this possibility and decided to interrupt progress. He noted that for a group acting as one people with one language, virtually anything was attainable. His solution: introduce multiple languages so that the builders could not effectively communicate. Confusion set in. The project could not be completed. A similar state of confusion exists in the world of technology today. Different parts of technological knowledge exist independently and side by side- without a unifying key to explain mutual relationships and shared impact. To find a new key it is useful to trace how the original came into being, how it became popular, how it guided technological evolution, and, eventually, how it was lost. It is a little known and fascinating history.

articleTitle: Joint optimization of process design and operational policies
abstract: Many traditional process improvement techniques focus on process design optimization without accounting for interactions between the process structure and operational policies used in during the process execution. This paper elaborates a mathematical programming model for simultaneous optimization of the process structure and process execution policies. The process optimization is considered as a part of multi-stage process improvement initiative what includes identification of process improvement options and their quantitative evaluation. The process design optimization is domain independent while process execution policies are problem area specific. In this paper, capacity planning policies for manufacturing processes are considered. The model is evaluated using an educational case study on manufacturing process optimization with increasing customer demand.

abstract: EVERY organization includes the innovation prevention department; it may or may not be visible, but it exists. It may include the CEO and upper level executives; managers from all the functional groups and at all levels; and the continuum from the new recruit to the technology professionals with years of technical contributions. Past innovators may also be in this group of naysayers. This innovation prevention department also includes a group of innovation killers; the organization's everyday practices and policies that govern performance.

articleTitle: Excellent execution: innovation, policy and regulation
abstract: THE successful execution of a plan to bring a radical or disruptive innovation (product or service) to market must include a strategy to influence policy and regulation. Why? Because innovation is always followed by regulation. Before there were mobile phones, there were no regulations about not texting and driving. The regulations necessarily follow the introduction of the innovative product or service because policy makers do not create regulations for products or services they have not yet imagined. (Hereafter, I'll simply refer to innovative products, but what I say is equally applicable to services.) And if your firm brings an innovative product to market, only to have its use curtailed by onerous regulations, then your firm has not successfully executed on its plan to bring that product to market. This article describes how you can influence policy and regulation.

abstract: I have been writing quarterly articles in the Engineering Management Review since 2011 and have covered many different topics that I believe technology managers should think about. If two of your engineers are having a conflict and you feel it in your gut that what you are about to tell them is going to make things worse, then listen to your gut and don't do it.

articleTitle: From engineer to manager, mastering the transition: effective delegation
abstract: Career progression is something all young professionals will experience. However, they can often find themselves facing major challenges for which they are underprepared. This type of role nominally comes with a significant increase in workload and responsibilities that elevate stress levels. Generally, their first attempt is to micromanage every activity, which results in an inefficient use of time. This becomes more evident as the team size and the complexity of the objectives grow and finally become impractical, leading to disastrous failures. An important aspect of leadership is the ability to effectively delegate tasks. Delegation involves handing over the authority, responsibility, and accountability for performing specific duties to others, so that they may act on your behalf. This article highlights six specific aspects of effective delegation for young professionals aspiring to become great managers and leaders.

articleTitle: Making the most of meetings
abstract: Running a meeting can seem difficult at first, but there a simple, basic steps you can take to ensure your meetings run smoothly and professionally-and are effective. Meetings are a key factor in moving a project or initiative forward. Good, well-organized meetings move things forward; poorly-organized meetings can set things back by days, weeks, or worse. There are some foundational elements that underpin an effective meeting. They are easy to master and, once you have, your meetings will be among the best-run in your organization.

articleTitle: Project excellence or failure? Doing is the best kind of learning
abstract: Project management<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</sup> has been around for decades. and has also evolved over time. Likewise, the author has worked for a few decades in Industry with a prime focus on project management. Various flavors and even evangelists exist, from PMI<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>, IPMA<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>, Prince2<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</sup>, Agile<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</sup> and more. The author has had experiences with several of these flavors. Unfortunately for many years, a substantial amount of projects still does not deliver on time, on budget or worse do not create the value expected. It has been published in various media and type of organizations, from research to industry and government for example by organizations such as The Standish Group and others. It seems that despite of all the project evaluations, we have not learned from all those past projects. Nor did all the development in methods and tools help us overcome this problem, or it might be due to other factors such as the human factor, as has been subject of the Dutch National Research Group (DNRG<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup>) on Project Management under the umbrella of IPMA. Why does this problem keep manifesting itself? And of course the question arises, how do we learn best? Time to rethink project management? The current article intends to provide Young Professionals some tips or at least food for thought, based on a personal retrospect based on just a few cases from the author's past experiences. In particular, it aims to give the members of the IEEE Young Professionals a perspective for a bright future, given the large number of technological, innovation, societal projects, and business ventures expected as we enter the era of digital transformation.

articleTitle: Learning to Become Better—“Backward Research” As a New Approach for Analyzing Organizations' Innovation Processes
abstract: This article introduces a new approach of learning where the innovation potential of an organization lies. “Backward Research” is a best practice approach from industry: it offers a tool for getting insights into corporate innovation processes. It leads to a new understanding of innovation procedures and developments, as many documented processes are different in daily practice. Organizations can use this approach to analyze their learning capabilities and to identify areas of improvement.

articleTitle: Assessing cultural influences in megaproject practices
abstract: Departing from traditional project management, this article focuses on cultural and localized differences and influences on a specific project activity, and furthermore on the specific influences on large important critical projects (also called "megaprojects"). It analyzes relevant methodologies, theories and results from other disciplines such as micro-behaviors influenced by local cultures, socio-cultural theories, cultural synergy processes and hybrid institutions, physioeconomics as well as different practices in contracting. It is shown that the very definitions of the concept of "megaproject" are diverse in the world, and details are given. A scaled gap analysis tool is proposed, rooted in the above theories and results, aiming at identifying cultural differences between megaprojects from a set of qualitative measures. To further allow for causal analysis, a set of cultural impact measures is proposed, and the same sample of international megaprojects is assessed correspondingly. The tool has allowed analyzing a sample of 16 documented international megaprojects on 5 continents. The taxonomy of the cultural attributes and causal impacts allows grouping the megaprojects by clusters of similar culturally driven management styles, irrespective of implementation countries. Taking thereafter the viewpoint of characterizing a given regional culture, it is shown that Scandinavian project management practices evidence a specific combination of cultural influence measures relying on hybrid governance and communications, unique work culture and tools, as well as an approach to adaptation. The paper finally discusses ethical characteristics of megaprojects, to conjecture that the alternatives are far fewer and more globalized. The conclusion shows that, despite the fact that to apprehend cultural factors in general is a very complex endeavor; the limited set of cultural influence measures identified here allows characterizing cultural impact on megaprojects. Megaprojects can be clustered or contrasted by cultural influences, by mana. This article focuses on cultural differences and influences on a specific project activity, and furthermore on the specific influences on the execution outcomes of large important critical projects (also called "megaprojects"). It analyzes relevant methodologies, theories and results from other disciplines such as cross-cultural analysis, micro-behaviors influenced by local cultures, sociocultural theories, cultural synergy processes and hybrid institutions, physioeconomics as well as different practices in contracting. It is shown that the very definitions of the concept of "megaproject" are diverse in the world, and details are given. A set of 16 megaproject cultural attributes, and of impact attributes, is proposed. A scaled gap analysis is enabled, rooted in the above theories and results, aiming at identifying cultural differences between megaprojects and project outcomes, from the proposed attributes. That analysis is applied to a sample of 16 documented international megaprojects on 5 continents. The taxonomy of the cultural attributes and causal impacts allows grouping the megaprojects by clusters of similar culturally driven management styles, irrespective of implementation countries and national cultures. Megaprojects can now be clustered or contrasted by cultural influences, by management styles, thus serving concrete needs in megaproject management Taking thereafter the viewpoint of characterizing a given regional culture, it is shown that Scandinavian project management practices evidence a specific combination of cultural influence measures relying on hybrid governance and communications, unique work culture and tools, as well as an approach to adaptation. The paper finally discusses ethical characteristics of megaprojects, to conjecture that the alternatives are few and more globalized.

abstract: LEADING the innovation team presents not only operational challenges, but perhaps more importantly, the challenges involved in integrating the team members who come with diverse personalities and different personal aspirations; competencies that need accommodation; and a many differences related to personal attitudes, characteristics, knowledge, and more.

articleTitle: Entrepreneurship your business plan
abstract: USUALLY you would contact investors with an introductory letter to initiate a discussion on financing, and send a business plan when asked. The hope is you'll be given the opportunity to make a PowerPoint presentation. We will discuss the business plan and briefly cover the PowerPoint presentation.

articleTitle: Telemedicine: determining "critical to quality" characteristics for a healthcare service system design based on a survey of physical rehabilitation providers
abstract: Purpose: This study examines the key attributes of telemedicine from the healthcare provider's perspective and to show how telemedicine may impact healthcare service delivery. Methodology: The study was based on a review of current telemedicine/ telehealth research and the analysis of data from a survey of healthcare professionals/providers in the physical rehabilitation sector. Using a six-sigma process development approach that identified "critical-to-quality" characteristics, the study identified specific telemedicine characteristics that healthcare service providers in the physical rehabilitation sector saw as being useful and essential. Findings: Empirical data from the survey indicated the application of telemedicine technologies can assist in making the delivery of healthcare services more efficient while maintaining the same high quality of service. Contribution: This study aided in determining what specific functions and capabilities healthcare providers would prefer to see in a telemedicine enabled service system design to achieve improved cost and time savings for both the patient and the provider. In view of the specialized area from which the data was obtained, healthcare providers were interested in viewing their patients in real time, communicating with them, and gathering relevant vital signs and treatment data meant for use in emergency and daily routine notifications and consultations.

articleTitle: Augmenting corporate R&D with networked micro innovation teams
abstract: Continuous innovation is key to a company's growth. The current models for corporate research and development are not suited for evaluating small scale emerging technology and trends. Networked micro innovation teams fill that gap and augment corporate R&D expenditure but using employee volunteers to identify and evaluate innovative concepts. These teams provide competitive advantages to the companies which develop them. The basic structure of corporate research and development has not changed despite radical changes in how ideas and technologies emerge in the market [1]. There is ample opportunity for companies to create internal innovation teams which evaluate emerging technologies and trends at a smaller scale than is practical with the traditional R&D departments. There are few studies among the legion about R&D which consider very small, or micro, innovations. Technology now enables a different approach to identifying and testing opportunities at a drastically smaller, cheaper scale than. In the past, innovative R&D departments have created autonomous islands free from bureaucracy or traditional management in order to address specific goals. Lockheed Martin's skunk work [2] and Alphabet's X lab (formerly Google[x]) are examples of innovation incubators outside the formal R&D process [3]. Creating separate laboratories which operate under separate rules can be useful pursuing auditions goals and for time and capital intensive projects, however, even these looser structures are overkill for the needs of some projects. To fill this gap, companies should create micro innovation teams which function as a network of local, decentralized teams. For example, buying an Oculus rift to explore its capabilities is an act too small for either a traditional or skunk works-style corporate R&D department. Yet, there are many opportunities for open innovation available to companies if they have the ability to conduct rapid and small-scale experimentation.

articleTitle: Better young than never: the what, why, and how of leadership for young professionals
abstract: It is natural for young professionals to start out following leaders and mentors, and this is the course many prefer. They are content to follow the usual progression, and move into leadership roles of their own later in their careers. That, they think, will be the time to learn how to lead teams to achieve organizational goals. Other young professionals, however, want to start learning leadership early. It can be daunting: Some early-career engineers may not yet have seen leaders in action long enough to understand leadership's challenges. Others may be overawed by the responsibility, and hold back, afraid risk putting themselves forward. Yet learning to lead early in one's career is valuable, even essential, to realizing one's full professional potential. This article will discuss what leadership means, why a young professional should become a leader, and how to get there.

articleTitle: Managing technical professionals: talent management
abstract: ONE quote we often hear during career discussions is that "we are responsible for our careers". While I do believe that this is true, I also believe that as managers we share the responsibility for the careers of our team members and that talent management is a critical aspect of our role as a manager.

articleTitle: Project to follow up and measure success of a significant process change
abstract: THE previous three columns introduced this series focused on projects with the mandate to put in place significant changes to the processes currently used by the organization, or to introduce a new process. The changes could be something needed in an established company, or maybe in a startup which is growing and now needs more formalized processes. While it is certainly possible to ask one project team to handle a single project to plan for the change, design and implement it, and follow up afterwards to determine the success of the new process, we have found it more productive to examine the stages individually. We have viewed that by establishing separate projects for the stages of the process change. The intention in this column is to discuss projects with the mandate to follow up after a significant process change has been put in place to determine whether or not the goals for the change have been met. For this project we will use a new example to illustrate he concepts.

articleTitle: On the fading of organizational interfaces in the era of Internet-of-Things
abstract: THE previous article discussed the adaptation from a Greek temple structure to the tightly packed atomic structure, when tackling the organizational issues related to the transformation of a (hardware) product centric company to the business-driven entity. It turned out that tight interaction is necessary if fast- evolving data-driven business services or software products are to be developed and marketed. Therefore, it might be interesting to investigate a unique approach nowadays often used in the software world: DevOps, a term first forged by Andrew Clay Shafer and Patrick Debois at the Agile 2008 conference [1].

articleTitle: Charles Proteus Steinmetz
abstract: AS engineers and managers of technology, we build on the technical accomplishments of our predecessors; their work becomes the technological foundation that allows us to pursue research and advance theory and practice related to the engineering profession.

articleTitle: Raising money
abstract: NEARLY $20 billion in venture capital is invested in the US per quarter! A closer examination of the statistics shows a majority of the investment goes into Web.2 and mobile applications and later stage startup companies; only a minuscule fraction goes into seed-stage hardware companies.

articleTitle: Practitioner competencies: technical + communication and leadership
abstract: THIS quote comes from an extensive interview with Robert Lutz who was then the Vice Chairman of Chrysler Corporation. His career included executive positions in engineering and product development at BMW, Ford, Chrysler, and General Motors. At each of these organizations, Lutz made significant contributions to engineering management and made major advances in the design of not only new cars, but more importantly many successful new car designs Lutz was asked, how he would evaluate the average engineer's performance relative to making a significant contribution to the organization.

articleTitle: Process projects
abstract: THIS and the subsequent few columns will address projects for which the product produced is process change. All projects involve change, clearly. While the products of most projects are often more tangible, process projects are legitimate projects with their own set of issues and problems. They can and should be managed in the same way that any project is managed, but they do require special considerations in order to be successful. Suggestions which can help with the success of such projects will be presented in this series of columns, and these will be illustrated via some examples of real or near-real projects. Given the space available for each of these columns, multiple columns are needed to be able to include both the suggestions and the examples. Some process projects involve planning for a process change, or a new process; others involve implementation of the process and still others involve follow-up once the (new) process (change) is in place. Or, perhaps the project spans all of these components. As for any project, knowledge of the business area of the project's product is one key to success.

articleTitle: Who cares? An opinion about stakeholder management
abstract: Many engineering curriculums comprise Project Management as a skill taught to students, and tools and methodologies are discussed broadly in corresponding communities. With large organizations continuing to span multiple cultures, geographies and professions, different opinions often need to be considered before making a decision. The article outlines the importance of considering balances of power and how to standardize on a process.

articleTitle: Project to plan for significant process change
abstract: THE previous column introduced this series focused on projects with the mandate to put in place significant changes to the processes currently used by the organization. While it is certainly possible to ask one project team, within a single project, to plan for the change, implement it, and follow up afterwards to determine the success, it will be more productive to examine the stages individually. We will do that by establishing separate projects for the stages of the process change. The intention in this column is to discuss projects with the mandate to plan for a significant process change. Two examples were described, one in a volunteer organization and the other in a company which has been operating for a few years, with the culture and processes slowly changing over time. These will be used as examples to illustrate the suggestions which can help to make such a project successful.

articleTitle: Managing technical professionals: applying management skills to other aspects of our lives
abstract: HAVING an aging family member diagnosed recently with Dementia, I have been reading articles, blogs, and various communications about the disease. The Friday before Easter, one of the weekly newsletters, I read regularly, had an article entitled "Focus on what really matters and soar above the clouds". It's a great article written by Angela Lunde in May 2014 and I recommend everyone to read it. It's not specifically about Dementia, but more about life and our attitude towards life in general; the general premise being "focus on what's important and let go of the smaller things that don't really matter", and it also shows how applying some of the critical skills we have all been trained to use at work could help us in our personal lives as well. It is this aspect of the article along with a recent experience I had in one of my new IEEE assignments that led me to write this quarter's article on "applying management skills to other aspects of our lives".

articleTitle: Managing technical professionals: how to react when one of your top performers decides to leave
abstract: ORGANIZATIONS depend on top performers to accomplish organizational goals. Top performers can be managers or individual contributors, and they distinguish themselves in the way they lead teams to successfully execute on projects, lead projects, or contribute to projects as technical contributors. And since organizations depend on these top performers they demonstrate their appreciation by assigning them the most challenging projects, giving them visibility to help them advance in their careers, keeping them satisfied financially by giving large bonuses, company stock, etc., and giving a positive message to the top performers that they are making a difference in the company and that they are valued in the organization.

articleTitle: Decision points in career and life: being a volunteer
abstract: During life there are decision points which can dramatically influence the future direction of our lives. Unlike typical scientific experiments there is no possibility to re-run the experiences and discover the result of making a different decision, so only speculation is available. After a discussion of the framework of these decision points, the author relates them to his own experiences as a volunteer, mainly in IEEE, and describes some opportunities which these created for him. It is based on a presentation given at an IEEE Student Branch event at University of Bath [1].

articleTitle: Excellent execution: top ten lessons for managers
abstract: IN this article, we'll focus on the lessons derived from some of the most downloaded articles from the IEEE Transactions on Engineering Management. Hundreds of engineering managers have voted with their download choices over many years.

articleTitle: Project to design and implement significant process change
abstract: THE previous two columns introduced this series focused on projects with the mandate to put in place significant changes to the processes currently used by the organization, or to introduce a new process, maybe in a startup which is growing and now needs more formalized processes. While it is certainly possible to ask one project team, within a single project, to plan for the change, design and implement it, and follow up to determine the success, it will be more productive to examine the stages individually.

articleTitle: Big data commercialization
abstract: We consider the emerging trade in big data through commercial transactions. Through a wide ranging systematic literature review that covers both academic and practitioner perspectives, we first demonstrate that there is increasing interest in big data commercialization, which mostly consists of exploratory theoretical development and managerial prescriptions to date. We outline the new types of businesses that seek to create and appropriate value, including the data supplier, data manager, data custodian, data aggregator, application developer and service provider. Building upon this typology, we discuss the processes of business model emergence, and the importance of data ecosystems, reviewing both ecosystem structure and dynamics. We also highlight the challenges for the trade in big data, including IP protection, regulatory complexity, pricing, the development of data agreements and privacy concerns. We conclude with an outline for future research.

articleTitle: Risk assessment using paired comparison expert judgment for ranking of compounding outsourcing facilities
abstract: Government regulators, like other managers and decision makers, are often faced with the challenge of completing a task or project with scarce resources. In such cases, decision makers must optimitize allocation of their insufficient resources to achieve the best outcome. For regulators like the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), optimitization of scarce audit resources is accomplished through ranking of individuals or institutions based on risks and other deciding factors. In this paper, we will discuss a novel application of the paired comparison expert judgment technique to develop a risk-ranking model that can allow FDA regulators to efficiently allocate their resources and focus on pharmacy compounding firms that could pose the greatest public health risk. Empirical research on the factors that can assess compounding risks is explored to understand their influences. Sensitivity analysis of these risk factors identified the top factors that had the most significant effect on the outcome of the quantitative risk assessment model. The resulting model from this research is inclusive as it was developed with inputs from experts from the federal and state governments, and also members of the pharmacy compounding industry. As such, it can be beneficial to stakeholders from both the private and public pharmacy compounding sectors.

articleTitle: Markov decision process for comparative economic analysis of immunization strategies against hepatitis A virus
abstract: Hepatitis A vaccination in the U.S. is currently universally recommended for all children between the ages of one and two years. Several nations have vaccination strategies which target high-risk groups or children who live in areas with high incidence rates of the disease, but developing countries often have no recommendations due to their poor economic conditions and the effect this may have on access to vaccinations. This study uses Markov decision process for baseline cost utility and comparative effectiveness analyses of various vaccination strategies to counter hepatitis A virus between a developed country (U.S.) and a developing country (Mexico). Treeage Pro Healthcare software was employed in Markov decision analysis. Secondary data was utilized in the model from available literature. Results showed that for the U.S., the universal vaccination strategy was the most cost effective while the no vaccination strategy was the lowest cost. Whereas, for Mexico the effectiveness for both no vaccination and universal strategies were almost the same, however, the cost of no vaccination was the lowest. The results could alter hepatitis A vaccination guidelines and decrease the large amount of indirect and directs costs of the disease, while also potentially eradicating the severe cases or deaths that occur as a result of infection.

articleTitle: James Clerk Maxwell (1831-1879)
abstract: James Clerk Maxwell, the celebrated Natural Philosopher and the father of electromagnetism, who laid the foundations for modern telecommunications theory, systems and applications, was born in 1831 in 14 India Street Edinburgh, Scotland. He was brought up at his father's country estate, Glenlair House in Dumfriesshire, Scotland, and he attended school at the Edinburgh Academy. Maxwell was a precocious child; he wrote his first paper on "Oval Curves", when he was only 14 years old. The paper was presented to the Royal Society of Edinburgh-Scotland's national academy-on his behalf by James Forbes, Professor of Natural Philosophy at the University of Edinburgh, in 1846.
